Take-home Exercise 01

Applying spatial and spatio-temporal point pattern analysis methods to identify factors affecting road traffic accidents in the Bangkok Metropolitan Region.

Author

Hung Thai

Published

September 17, 2026

Modified

September 27, 2026

1 Assignment: Geospatial analytics for Public safety

Reference: ISSS626 Take-home Exercise 1: Geospatial Analytics for Public Safety

2 Overview

This take-home exercise investigates the spatial and/or spatio-temporal patterns of public-safety point events using road traffic accidents within the Bangkok Greater Metropolitan Area.

The object of the exercise are:

  • To prepare and integrate real-world geospatial and temporal data for spatial and spatio-temporal point-pattern analysis.

  • To investigate first-order properties of the point pattern by examining how the intensity or distribution of events varies across space and/or time.

  • To investigate second-order properties by examining whether events exhibit evidence of spatial or spatio-temporal interaction, such as clustering, inhibition, or approximate randomness.

  • To critically evaluate the analytical assumptions, methodological choices, and limitations associated with the selected point-pattern methods.

  • To communicate the analytical findings effectively through appropriate geovisualisation and geocommunication.

  • To translate the analytical evidence into meaningful implications for public-safety planning and management.

3 The data

The following 3 datasets will be used in this exercise.

Dataset Name Description Format Source
Thailand Road Accident [2019-2022] Data on road accidents in Thailand, including details on location, severity, and date of incidents. CSV Kaggle
Thailand Roads (OpenStreetMap Export) OpenStreetMap Geospatial data of Thailand. ESRI Shapefile Humanitarian Data Exchange (HDX)
Thailand - Subnational Administrative Boundaries Boundaries of Thailand’s Geospatial dataset. ESRI Shapefile Humanitarian Data Exchange (HDX)

About Thailand Road Accident dataset

This dataset provides comprehensive statistics on recorded road accidents in Thailand, spanning from approximately 2019 to 2022. The data was sourced from raw information provided by the Office of the Permanent Secretary, Ministry of Transport, which is also utilized in this public dashboard for easier access and visualization. The dataset encompasses various aspects of road accidents and aims to shed light on the trends and patterns within this critical area of concern, analysis of this data could be crucial in guiding road safety policies and measures.

Column Description
acc_code The accident code or identifier.
incident_datetime The date and time of the accident occurrence.
report_datetime The date and time when the accident was reported.
province_th The name of the province in Thailand, written in Thai.
province_en The name of the province in Thailand, written in English.
agency The government agency responsible for the road and traffic management.
route The route or road segment where the accident occurred.
vehicle_type The type of vehicle involved in the accident.
presumed_cause The presumed cause or reason for the accident.
accident_type The type or nature of the accident.
number_of_vehicles_involved The number of vehicles involved in the accident.
number_of_fatalities The number of fatalities resulting from the accident.
number_of_injuries The number of injuries resulting from the accident.
weather_condition The weather condition at the time of the accident.
latitude The latitude coordinate of the accident location.
longitude The longitude coordinate of the accident location.
road_description The description of the road type or configuration where the accident occurred.
slope_description The description of the slope condition at the accident location.

The original data has total 81735 accident records in all over Thailand from 2019-2022.

4 Data preparation

Install and load R packages

pacman::p_load(readr, dplyr, lubridate, ggplot2, tmap, sf, spNetwork, spatstat, plotly, gtsummary, sparr, terra, tidyr, tidyverse)
Noteset reproducibility value

In order to ensures that stochastic algorithms and randomized spatial processes yield identical results every time the workflow runs, we need to set reproducibility value.

set.seed(1234)

Import road traffic accident data

Loading Thailand road traffic accidents 2019-2022.

bmr_acc <- read_csv(
  "data/thai_road_accident_2019_2022.csv",
  show_col_types = FALSE
)

Checking for missing values

null_counts <-   sum(is.na(bmr_acc))
null_counts
[1] 718

The dataset contains 718 missing values in total. We will check for missing values in each column to identify which columns have missing data. Listing the number of missing values for each column in the dataset

data.frame(
  Column = colnames(bmr_acc),
  Missing_Values = colSums(is.na(bmr_acc))
)

There are 359 missing values in the latitude column and 359 missing values in the longitude column. Since these columns are crucial for spatial analysis, we will remove rows with missing values in these columns.

From Wikipedia, Bangkok Metropolitan Region (BMR) is the capital and most populous city of Thailand. It is located in the central part of the country, on the Chao Phraya River delta. The BMR consists of Bangkok and its surrounding provinces, including Nonthaburi, Pathum Thani, Samut Prakan, Nakhon Pathom, and Samut Sakhon. The dataset contains information on the location, severity, and date of accidents, which will be used for spatial and spatio-temporal point-pattern analysis.

bmr_acc_sf <- bmr_acc %>%
  filter(province_en == "Bangkok" | province_en == "Nonthaburi" | province_en == "Pathum Thani" | province_en == "Samut Prakan" | province_en == "Nakhon Pathom" | province_en == "Samut Sakhon") %>%
  #filter(year(incident_datetime) == 2022) %>%
  filter(!is.na(longitude), !is.na(latitude)) %>%
  st_as_sf(coords = c("longitude", "latitude"), crs = 4326) %>%
  st_transform(crs = 32647) # UTM Zone 47N (EPSG:32647) for Bangkok Metropolitan Region

Verifying that the missing values have been removed

null_counts_after <- sum(is.na(bmr_acc_sf))
null_counts_after
[1] 0

Next we check for duplicate records in the dataset. Duplicate records can skew the analysis and lead to inaccurate results. We will identify and remove any duplicate rows based on the acc_code column, which serves as a unique identifier for each accident.

# Check for duplicate records based on the 'acc_code' column
duplicates <- bmr_acc_sf[duplicated(bmr_acc_sf$acc_code), ]
nrow(duplicates)
[1] 0

There are 0 duplicate records in the dataset based on the acc_code column. Therefore, no further action is needed to remove duplicates. In case there were duplicates, we would remove them using the following code:

Removing duplicate records

# Saving the cleaned and filtered road traffic accident data for the Bangkok Metropolitan Region in RDS format for future use.
#| echo: false
#| eval: false
#saveRDS(bmr_acc_sf, file = "data/bmr_road_traffic_accidents_2019-2022.rds")
bmr_acc_sf <- readRDS("data/bmr_road_traffic_accidents_2019-2022.rds")

Import Thailand road network data from OpenStreetMap

Import road network data for Thailand from OpenStreetMap using the sf package.

thailand_roads <- st_read(dsn = "data/hotosm_tha_roads_lines_shp.shp", layer = "hotosm_tha_roads_lines_shp") %>%
  st_set_crs(4326) %>% # Set the coordinate reference system to WGS 84 (EPSG:4326)
  st_transform(crs = 32647) # UTM Zone 47N (EPSG:32647) for Bangkok Metropolitan Region
Reading layer `hotosm_tha_roads_lines_shp' from data source `C:\hungthq\ISSS626-GAA\Take-home_Ex\Take-home_Ex01\data\hotosm_tha_roads_lines_shp.shp' using driver `ESRI Shapefile' Simple feature collection with 2833401 features and 14 fields Geometry type: MULTILINESTRING Dimension:     XY Bounding box:  xmin: 97.33814 ymin: 5.643645 xmax: 105.6528 ymax: 20.47168 Geodetic CRS:  WGS 84

The road network data contains ~2.8M road segments in Thailand. We will filter the data to include only the road segments within the Bangkok Metropolitan Region (BMR) for spatial analysis.

bmr_roads_orig <- thailand_roads %>%
  st_intersection(bmr_adm_boundary) # Filter road segments within the BMR
NoteNote

The geospatial data is in the form of MULTILINESTRING geometries, which represent the road segments as lines. To simplify the analysis, we will convert the MULTILINESTRING geometries to LINESTRING geometries using the st_cast() function from the sf package. This will allow us to work with individual road segments as separate features.

bmr_roads <- bmr_roads_orig %>%
  st_cast("LINESTRING") # Convert MULTILINESTRING to LINESTRING geometries

Observing the attributes of the BMR road network data, we can see that it contains information about the road segments, including their names, types, and geometries. This data will be useful for spatial analysis and visualization of road traffic accidents in relation to the road network. For further analysis, we will focus on the road segments that are classified as “primary” roads, which are major roads that connect different regions and are likely to have higher traffic volumes. We will filter the data to include only these primary road segments for spatial analysis from “highway” attribute.

Displaying the unique values in the “highway” attribute to identify the different types of roads in the BMR road network data.

unique(bmr_roads$highway)
[1] "steps"          "footway"        "secondary"      "service"        "residential"    "primary"        "tertiary_link"  "path"           "secondary_link" "pedestrian"     [11] "tertiary"       "primary_link"   "unclassified"   "corridor"       "cycleway"       "busway"         "construction"   "motorway_link"  "track"          "trunk_link"     [21] "trunk"          "motorway"       "proposed"       "road"           "raceway"        "platform"

Identify road type for each accident event

bmr_roads <- read_rds("data/bmr_roads.rds")
bmr_acc_sf <- read_rds("data/bmr_road_traffic_accidents_2019-2022.rds")
# 1. index of the nearest road segment for every accident
nearest_idx <- st_nearest_feature(bmr_acc_sf, bmr_roads)
# 2. attach highway type + snapping distance
bmr_acc_sf <- bmr_acc_sf %>%
  mutate(
    highway = bmr_roads$highway[nearest_idx],
    dist_to_road_m = as.numeric(
      st_distance(bmr_acc_sf, bmr_roads[nearest_idx, ], by_element = TRUE)),
    # 3. only trust the match if the accident is close to the road
    highway = if_else(dist_to_road_m <= 50, highway, "off-network (>50 m)")
  )

table(bmr_acc_sf$highway)

  geom_col(fill = "steelblue") +

  coord_flip() + # Flips the chart horizontally for readable labels
  labs(
    title = "Number of Accidents per Highway Type",
    x = "Highway Type",
    y = "Number of Accidents"
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  # Add exact counts to the end of each bar
  geom_text(aes(label = n), hjust = -0.2, size = 3.5) +
  # Expand y-axis slightly so the text labels don't get cut off
  scale_y_continuous(expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0.1)))

For the study purpose, we will focus on the primary roads in the BMR road network data. The primary roads are classified as “motoway”, “trunk”, “primary”, “secondary”. We will filter the data to include only these primary road segments for spatial analysis.

bmr_roads_filtered <- bmr_roads %>%
  select("highway") %>% 
  filter(highway %in% hw_types)

5 Exploratory Data Analysis (EDA)

In this section, we will perform exploratory data analysis (EDA) on the road traffic accident data for the Bangkok Metropolitan Region (BMR). The goal of EDA is to understand the distribution and characteristics of the data, identify patterns and trends, and detect any anomalies or outliers that may affect the analysis.

5.1 Overall plot

The overall plot provides a visual summary of the road traffic accidents in the Bangkok Metropolitan Region (BMR) for the year 2019 to 2022. It overlays the administrative boundaries, primary road network, and accident locations, allowing us to quickly identify areas with high accident density and their relation to major roads.

Observing the map, we can see that the majority of accidents are concentrated along the primary roads and in densely populated areas, highlighting the importance of focusing on these regions for traffic safety interventions.

This insight indicates that the 6 road types classified as primary roads are the most critical areas to target for traffic safety improvements and accident prevention measures.

6 First-order Spatial Analysis

In this section, we will perform a first-order spatial analysis to understand the distribution of road traffic accidents in the Bangkok Metropolitan Region.

# Build owin from the BMR union, and convert to ppp
bmr_owin <- as.owin(st_union(bmr_adm_boundary))
acc_ppp  <- as.ppp(st_coordinates(bmr_acc_sf), W = bmr_owin)

#acc_ppp        # summary: check n, window area, units
plot(acc_ppp, main = "BMR 2019 - 2022 Accidents")

6.1 Clark-Evans Test for Nearest neighbor analysis

clark_evans_test <- clarkevans.test(acc_ppp,
  correction="none",
  clipregion = bmr_owin,
  alternative = "clustered"
  )
clark_evans_test

    Clark-Evans test
    No edge correction
    Z-test

data:  acc_ppp
R = 0.15189, p-value < 2.2e-16
alternative hypothesis: clustered (R < 1)
Note

The results provide overwhelmingly strong evidence that your traffic accidents are highly clustered rather than randomly scattered across the region. Here is the breakdown of the two key metrics:

  • The R-value (0.30091): The Clark-Evans index (\(R\)) measures the distance between nearest neighbors. An \(R\) value of 1.0 means complete spatial randomness, while values greater than 1 mean points are evenly dispersed. Your value of roughly 0.152 is well below 1, meaning the accidents are highly clustered. On average, the distance between any accident and its nearest neighbor is only 15.2% of what it would be if they were distributed entirely at random.
  • The p-value (< 2.2e-16): This is the smallest p-value R can display, essentially zero. It means the probability of this clustered pattern happening by random chance is virtually non-existent. We can confidently reject the null hypothesis of complete spatial randomness (CSR).

To visualize the exact locations of those clusters, we create a Kernel Density Estimation (KDE) map using the spatstat package.

Calculate the KDE to visualize accident clusters.

# Calculate the kernel density estimate
acc_kde <- density(acc_ppp, sigma = 0.1)
plot(acc_kde, main = "BMR 2019-2022 Accidents - KDE")

# add the regional boundary on top for context
plot(bmr_owin, add = TRUE, lwd = 1.5, border = "yellow")

6.2 Quadrat Analysis

Note

Quadrat analysis is a foundational spatial statistics method used to determine whether a set of points (like your traffic accidents) is randomly distributed, clustered, or evenly dispersed across a study area.

Here is how it works:

  • The Grid: The study area is divided into a grid of equal-sized sub-regions, called “quadrats” (like laying a checkerboard over your map of the Bangkok Metropolitan Region).

  • The Count: The algorithm counts the number of points that fall inside each quadrat.

  • The Comparison: It compares the observed counts against what you would expect if the points were completely random (Complete Spatial Randomness, or CSR).

# Define the number of quadrats along x and y directions
nx <- 10
ny <- 10

# Perform quadrat count
quadrat_counts <- quadratcount(acc_ppp, nx = nx, ny = ny)

6.5 First-order SPPA at province level

Create owin object for the study window based on 6 provinces separately.

# Create owin objects for each province after projecting to the appropriate CRS
Bangkok_owin <- Bangkok %>%
  st_transform(crs = 32647) %>%
  as.owin()

Nonthaburi_owin <- Nonthaburi %>%
  st_transform(crs = 32647) %>%
  as.owin()
Pathum_Thani_owin <- Pathum_Thani %>%
  st_transform(crs = 32647) %>%
  as.owin()
Samut_Prakan_owin <- Samut_Prakan %>%
  st_transform(crs = 32647) %>%
  as.owin()
Nakhon_Pathom_owin <- Nakhon_Pathom %>%
  st_transform(crs = 32647) %>%
  as.owin()
Samut_Sakhon_owin <- Samut_Sakhon %>%
  st_transform(crs = 32647) %>%
  as.owin()

# Combine point events and study window for each province
Bangkok_ppp <- acc_ppp[Bangkok_owin]

Samut_Sakhon_ppp <- acc_ppp[Samut_Sakhon_owin]

Clark-Evans test for spatial randomness of accidents in each province.

clark_evans_bangkok <- clarkevans.test(Bangkok_ppp, correction = "none", clipregion = Bangkok_owen, alternative = "two.sided", nsim = 999)

7 Second-Order Spatial Point Pattern Analysis

7.1 Analysis usinng G-function

Calculating G-function estimation

# ---- G-function ----
G_acc <- Gest(acc_ppp, correction = "border")
plot(G_acc, xlim = c(0, 500))

Performing complete spatial randomness test

G_acc.csr <- envelope(acc_ppp, Gest, nsim = 99, rank = 1, global = FALSE)
plot(G_acc.csr)

7.2 Analysis using F-function

Calculating F-function estimation

# ---- F-function ----
F_acc <- Fest(acc_ppp)
plot(F_acc)

Performing complete spatial randomness test

F_acc.csr <- envelope(acc_ppp, Fest, nsim = 99, rank = 1, global = FALSE)
plot(F_acc.csr)

Note

inteprete of the f-function csr test:

  • Observed vs. Theoretical: The solid black line representing observed data, \(\hat{F}_{obs}(r)\), sits substantially below the red dashed line representing Complete Spatial Randomness, \(F_{theo}(r)\).

  • Empty Space Interpretation: The F-function measures the distance from a randomly selected point in empty space to the nearest event (accident). Because the observed curve is lower than the theoretical curve, it means that if we pick a random spot on the map, the probability of an accident being within distance \(r\) is much lower than expected under a random distribution. This occurs because the points are tightly clumped together, leaving exceptionally large areas of empty space.

  • Statistical Significance: The red theoretical curve is tightly hugged by the grey simulation envelopes, \(\hat{F}_{hi}(r)\) and \(\hat{F}_{lo}(r)\). Because the observed black line falls entirely outside of these upper and lower bounds across the chart, the deviation from spatial randomness is highly statistically significant.

7.3 Analysis using K-function & L-funcion

Calculating K-function estimation

# ---- K-function ----
K_acc <- Kest(acc_ppp, correction = "Ripley")
plot(K_acc, . - r ~ r, ylab = "K(d)-r", xlab = "d(m)")

# ---- L-function ----
L_acc <- Lest(acc_ppp, correction = "Ripley")
plot(L_acc, . - r ~ r, ylab = "L(d)-r", xlab = "d(m)")

Performing complete spatial randomness test

K_acc.csr <- envelope(acc_ppp, Kest, nsim = 99, rank = 1, global = FALSE)
plot(K_acc.csr, . - r ~ r, xlab = "d", ylab = "K(d)-r")

L_acc.csr <- envelope(acc_ppp, Lest, nsim = 99, rank = 1, global = FALSE)
plot(L_acc.csr, . - r ~ r, xlab = "d", ylab = "L(d)-r")

8 Integration and Interpretation

8.1 What does the first-order analysis reveal about event intensity or distribution?

Your first-order analysis shows that accident intensity across the Bangkok Metropolitan Region is strongly inhomogeneous. Accidents pile up in a small number of core areas instead of spreading evenly.

The quadrat test rejects uniform intensity decisively. X² = 20,675 on 88 df, p < 2.2e-16. The counts themselves tell the story better than the test statistic, and your write-up could say so:

- The 89 tiles hold about 12,986 accidents, roughly 146 per tile on average.
- The actual counts run from 0 to 1,186. 13 tiles are completely empty, and several more have only 1–3 accidents.
- The 13 busiest tiles, about 15% of the area, hold roughly 63% of all accidents (about 8,180).
- The heaviest tiles (1,186, 822, 797, 695, 689, 623, 586, 556) sit together in rows 4–8, columns 5–9.
- That’s a contiguous high-intensity core, not scattered spikes.
- The edge tiles (rows 1, 9–10, column 1) are close to empty, so intensity drops sharply away from the core.

The Clark-Evans ratio confirms strong clustering. R ≈ 0.19 for the whole region, far below 1.

The province-level results show that intensity differs within each province too. Every province is significantly clustered, and the degree varies:

Province R
Bangkok 0.12 (most clustered)
Samut Prakan 0.14
Samut Sakhon 0.24
Pathum Thani 0.25
Nakhon Pathom 0.29
Nonthaburi 0.39 (least clustered)

Bangkok and Samut Prakan have the most concentrated patterns, which fits dense urban arterials and expressway corridors. Nonthaburi’s accidents are comparatively more spread out.

8.2 What does the second-order analysis reveal about interaction among events?

The observed G function lies far above the CSR envelope at every distance shown. Accidents have nearest neighbours much closer than they would if they were randomly scattered, so the null hypothesis of complete spatial randomness is rejected in favour of clustering.

Reading the curve

Ĝ(r) is the proportion of accidents whose nearest neighbouring accident is within r metres.

Distance r Observed Ĝ(r) Under CSR
~3 m ~0.30 ~0.00
10 m ~0.48 ~0.00
20 m ~0.58 ~0.00
50 m ~0.76 ~0.01
100 m ~0.86 ~0.05
~143 m ~0.90 ~0.10

  • Clustering at very short range: about half of all accidents have another accident within roughly 10 m, and about three-quarters within roughly 50 m. Under CSR almost none would.

  • The gap is huge at every distance: the envelope (grey band) is so narrow that the result isn’t borderline anywhere. The observed curve is 9 to 50 times the theoretical value across the whole range. The outcome is obvious, the accident events are very clusterly distributed.

  • Rapid rise, then a plateau: the curve climbs steeply below 30 m and levels off around 0.9. So about 10% of accidents have no neighbour within ~143 m. These are probably the isolated accidents in the sparse outer tiles your quadrat analysis found.

8.3 How do the first-order and second-order findings complement each other?

The two analyses answer different questions, and together they give a fuller picture than either one alone.

  • First-order (quadrat test, KDE, province-level analysis) answers where and how many: how accident intensity varies across the region.

  • Second-order answers how close together: whether accidents occur near other accidents more than chance would predict.

Common result between the 2 methods

Both reject complete spatial randomness, using independent evidence:

  • First-order: quadrat counts range from 0 to 1,186 per tile. About 15% of the area holds about 63% of accidents. The Clark-Evans ratio is about 0.19.

  • Second-order: about half of all accidents have another accident within roughly 10 m, while random scattering would give almost none.

They describe clustering at different scales:

  • Regional scale (kilometres), from first-order

  • Local scale (metres), from second-order

8.4 Are the findings consistent across different analytical views?

The findings are consistent across analytical views in their main conclusion. The Clark-Evans tests (overall and for each province), the quadrat test, KDE and the G function all reject complete spatial randomness and indicate strong clustering, with Bangkok the most concentrated province. The KDE bandwidth comparison shows that the apparent hotspot pattern depends on scale: broad regional concentration at kilometre bandwidths and site-level black spots at tens of metres, a scale that matches the G-function results. Consistency over time is supported only visually by the faceted maps. Formal spatio-temporal testing and inhomogeneous second-order analysis are still needed to confirm that the clustering is stable over time and not simply a product of uneven intensity along the road network.

8.5 What assumptions or limitations should be considered when interpreting the results?

These results should be interpreted with several limitations in mind. First, the analysis treats space as a continuous plane, whereas accidents are confined to the road network; combined with a homogeneous CSR null model, this biases all tests toward detecting clustering and prevents first-order concentration from being separated from genuine interaction between events. Second, the data contain many near-duplicate coordinates and exclude records with missing locations, and may under-represent roads outside national highway jurisdiction. Third, without traffic volume data, intensity reflects accident counts rather than risk. Finally, the results depend on the analyst’s choices of study window, quadrat grid and KDE bandwidth, and edge effects were not corrected. Network-constrained and inhomogeneous methods, exposure-adjusted rates, and spatio-temporal analysis would strengthen the conclusions.

8.6 Are there alternative explanations for the observed patterns?

The accidents might appear clustered for several reasons rather than a single underlying cause:

  • Physical Layout: Crashes naturally concentrate in high-traffic areas, busy intersections, and major highway junctions.

  • Data Quirks: Location tracking might be imprecise (pinning multiple accidents to one general landmark), and local roads might be missing from the dataset entirely.

  • Time Compression: Plotting four years of data at once makes accidents look grouped, even if they happened months or years apart. Only crashes happening at the exact same time and place (like a pile-up) are genuinely connected.

  • Peak Periods: Weekend and holiday spikes could just mean more cars are on the road, stricter police reporting, or increased drunk driving.

9.2 Network KDE on the primary road (highest value)

lixels  <- lixelize_lines(bmr_primary_roads, 500, mindist = 250)
samples <- lines_center(lixels)

nkde <- nkde(bmr_primary_roads, events = bmr_acc_sf,
                  w = rep(1, nrow(bmr_acc_sf)), samples = samples,
                  kernel_name = "quartic", bw = 300, div = "bw",
                  method = "simple", digits = 1, tol = 1,
                  grid_shape = c(10, 10), max_depth = 8,
                  agg = 5, sparse = TRUE, verbose = FALSE)

lixels$density <- nkde * 1000   # accidents per km of road
nz   <- lixels$density[lixels$density > 0]          
brks <- unique(c(0, quantile(nz, c(0.5, 0.75, 0.9, 0.95, 0.99)), max(nz)))
pal  <- c("#fee5d9", "#fcae91", "#fb6a4a", "#de2d26", "#a50f15", "#67000d")[seq_len(length(brks) - 1)]

tm_shape(bmr_district) + tm_borders(col = "grey85") +
  tm_shape(filter(lixels, density == 0)) + tm_lines(col = "grey85", lwd = 0.5) +
  tm_shape(filter(lixels, density > 0) %>% arrange(density)) +
  tm_lines(col = "density", lwd = 2,
           col.scale  = tm_scale_intervals(breaks = brks, values = pal),
           col.legend = tm_legend(title = "NKDE density")) +
  tm_title("Network KDE of road accidents, BMR (bw = 300 m)")
Note

Interpretation

  • Accidents concentrate on a few segments. 68% of the primary road network had no accident within 300 m in 2022. The darkest class, the top 1% of segments that have accidents (about 35 km), carries the highest density. This confirms the segment-scale clustering the G-function found.

  • The main hotspot is the eastern expressway corridor. It runs north–south along eastern Bangkok and then south-east through Khan Na Yao, Saphan Sung, Prawet and Lat Krabang, the same districts that top the per-km² choropleth.

9.3 Road accidents during Thais New-Year period (Songkran 11-17 Apr)

Based on EDA, we saw that the accidents increased significantly in Apr, it could related to 7 dangerous days 11-17 Apr - Songkran holidays.

# 1. Accidents per calendar day
daily_acc <- bmr_acc_sf %>%
  st_drop_geometry() %>%
  mutate(date = as_date(incident_datetime)) %>%
  count(date, name = "n_acc") %>%
  complete(date = seq(as_date("2019-01-01"), as_date("2022-12-31"), by = "day"),
           fill = list(n_acc = 0)) %>%
  mutate(songkran = if_else(month(date) == 4 & day(date) %in% 11:17, "Songkran", "Normal"),
         songkran = factor(songkran, levels = c("Normal", "Songkran")))
# 2. Average accidents per day
avg_acc <- daily_acc %>%
  group_by(songkran) %>%
  summarise(n_days      = n(),
            total_acc   = sum(n_acc),
            avg_per_day = mean(n_acc),
            sd          = sd(n_acc), .groups = "drop") %>%
  mutate(ratio_vs_normal = avg_per_day / avg_per_day[songkran == "Normal"])

Note

On average, the Bangkok Metropolitan Region had 12.25 road accidents per day during Songkran (11–17 April), against 6.94 on normal days between 2019 and 2022. That is about 1.77 times as many, or 77% more accidents per day. The seven-day holiday period is a clear temporal hotspot.

10 Public-Safety Planning and Management

Transportation and road-safety planning

Road-safety planning should work at two spatial scales. At the regional scale, the KDE and district choropleths identify where planning effort should be concentrated: central Bangkok. At the site scale, the G-function shows that accidents recur at specific points, along the main roads and intersections where targeted interventions can be implemented.

Emergency response planning

The strong spatial and temporal concentration supports demand-based deployment of emergency resources. Ambulances and rescue units can be pre-positioned near persistent hotspots.Deployment can also be scaled up during the peak periods identified in the EDA: Friday and Saturday evenings, and the April (Songkran) and December (New Year) holiday periods.

Public-safety policy

Because hot spots and road corridors cross provincial boundaries, policy should be coordinated across the six provinces and the agencies responsible for different road classes, supported by a shared, standardised accident database.

Cautions for decision-makers

These recommendations rest on accident counts in planar space, pooled over 2019–2022, and may not fully capture dynamic changes in traffic patterns, road conditions, or enforcement measures. Decision-makers should complement this analysis with real-time data and local knowledge to ensure effective and context-sensitive interventions.
